issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s possession becomes adverse to another co-sharer only upon a sufficiently clear ouster, and prolonged possession or municipal mutation alone does not establish ouster.
material_facts: The defendants claimed long and uninterrupted possession and asserted that one predecessor had possessed the property exclusively.
The parties’ predecessor interests may have remained co-sharers because it was unresolved whether the property had been partitioned by metes and bounds.
The defendants did not specifically plead when possession became adverse to the other co-sharers, and the High Court made no finding identifying when adverse possession began.
The High Court relied on municipal records, non-payment of rent or taxes, and an asserted open ouster, but did not explain how these established denial of the other co-sharers’ title.
The Supreme Court observed that possession by one co-sharer is ordinarily on behalf of all, and that possession might have been permissive or based on an arrangement.
issues.conclusion: The findings that the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession could not stand: the record did not establish the clear ouster and hostile possession required against co-sharers. The judgment was set aside and the matter remitted for fresh consideration; the Supreme Court did not finally determine title.
issues.legal_principle: Possession by one co-sharer is presumed to be on behalf of the others. Ouster requires denial of the other co-sharers’ title, hostile animus, long and uninterrupted possession, and open exercise of exclusive ownership to their knowledge. Mere non-participation in rent or profits, long possession, or mutation in one co-sharer’s name is insufficient by itself. The Court relied on Karbalai Begum v. Mohd. Sayeed, Annasaheb Bapusaheb Patil v. Balwant, Vidya Devi v. Prem Prakash, P. Lakshmi Reddy, Mohd. Zainulabudeen v. Sayed Ahmed Mohideen, and Darshan Singh v. Gujjar Singh.

rule.if: co_sharer_title_dispute and one_co_sharer_in_possession and not clear_hostile_ouster

predicates.co_sharer_title_dispute: The dispute concerns title to property claimed by people whose interests may be those of co-sharers.
predicates.one_co_sharer_in_possession: One co-sharer or that co-sharer’s predecessor possessed the commonly claimed property.
predicates.clear_hostile_ouster: The possessor clearly denied the other co-sharers’ title and openly exercised exclusive ownership to their knowledge.

issues.definition: When a title dispute concerns co-sharers and one co-sharer possesses the property without a clear hostile ouster, ouster is not established.

issues.legal_issue: In a title suit governed by the 1963 limitation law, a plaintiff who proves title need not also prove possession within the twelve years preceding suit; the defendant relying on adverse possession must establish it.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of title to the property and relief against a person occupying it.
The first appellate court required the plaintiff to prove title and possession within twelve years before filing suit and treated the claim as time-barred.
The High Court upheld that approach, while the Supreme Court identified it as an error in applying the limitation law.
The Supreme Court did not itself finally determine whether the plaintiff had proved title and remitted the matter for reconsideration.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts applied the wrong principle under Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963. If the plaintiff proves title, the defendant must establish adverse possession to defeat that title; the plaintiff need not prove possession within the period preceding suit.
issues.legal_principle: Article 65 of the Limitation Act, 1963 changed the position under Articles 142 and 144 of the Limitation Act, 1908: in a suit governed by Article 65, the plaintiff succeeds upon proving title, and the defendant bears the burden of proving adverse possession. The defendant must also prove animus possidendi.

predicates.title_suit: The proceeding is a suit seeking relief on the basis of title to property.
predicates.plaintiff_proves_title: The plaintiff establishes title to the property.

issues.definition: When a plaintiff proves title in a title suit, the defendant must prove adverse possession to defeat the claim.

issues.legal_issue: A decision in a prior rent-recovery suit does not bar a later title claim by res judicata when the prior suit determined only whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and did not decide title or adverse possession.
material_facts: The plaintiff had earlier brought a money suit seeking rent from the occupant, and that suit was dismissed after the plaintiff failed to show that the occupant had been inducted by the plaintiff or the plaintiff’s predecessors.
The defendants argued that the dismissal barred the later title suit by res judicata.

The Supreme Court held that the earlier suit could determine whether the occupant was the plaintiff’s tenant, but could not determine title or whether the defendants had acquired title by adverse possession.
issues.conclusion: The dismissal of the earlier money suit did not operate as res judicata on the questions of title or adverse possession.
issues.legal_principle: Res judicata does not bar a later determination of title or adverse possession where the earlier rent-recovery proceeding determined only the alleged tenancy and did not adjudicate those questions.

predicates.later_title_suit: The later proceeding seeks a determination of title to property.
predicates.prior_rent_recovery_suit: An earlier proceeding sought recovery of rent from the property’s occupant.
predicates.prior_suit_decided_only_tenancy: The earlier proceeding determined only whether the occupant was the claimant’s tenant and did not decide title or adverse possession.

issues.definition: A prior rent-recovery suit that decided only tenancy does not bar a later title determination.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court deciding a second appeal must formulate the substantial questions of law that arise for decision.
material_facts: The High Court dismissed a second appeal without formulating substantial questions of law.

The Supreme Court identified substantial questions that required consideration, including whether a registered partition was acted upon, whether possession was exclusive or permissive, and what rights were transferred.
The Supreme Court set aside the High Court judgment and remitted the matter for decision after proper questions of law were framed.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have formulated the substantial questions of law under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; the matter was remitted for fresh consideration on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 requires the High Court, in a second appeal, to formulate the substantial questions of law arising in the appeal before deciding it.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.substantial_questions_not_formulated: The High Court decides the second appeal without formulating the substantial questions of law arising in it.

issues.definition: When a second appeal is decided without formulating its substantial questions of law, those questions must be formulated.
